source_text: Force-march fifty miles for an advantage, and you will lose your lead commander. Only half your force will arrive.
modern_text: 9. If you march fifty li in order to outmanœuver the enemy, you will lose the leader of your first division, and only half your force will reach the goal.

location: Chapter VI (Weak Points and Strong), para 21
source_text: 21. Though according to my estimate the soldiers of Yüeh exceed our own in number, that shall advantage them nothing in the matter of victory. I say then that victory can be achieved.
modern_text: Even if the enemy outnumbers us, that advantage counts for nothing if we control the terms of engagement. Victory can be engineered.

source_text: Sun Tzu said: When launching a major military operation — a thousand fast chariots, a thousand heavy chariots, a hundred thousand armored soldiers, with supplies for a long campaign — the total cost at home and in the field, including diplomatic expenses, equipment maintenance, and vehicle and armor repairs, will reach a thousand ounces of silver per day. That is the price of fielding an army of 100,000.
modern_text: 1. Sun Tzŭ said: In the operations of war, where there are in the field a thousand swift chariots, as many heavy chariots, and a hundred thousand mail-clad soldiers, with provisions enough to carry them a thousand li, the expenditure at home and at the front, including entertainment of guests, small items such as glue and paint, and sums spent on chariots and armour, will reach the total of a thousand ounces of silver per day. Such is the cost of raising an army of 100,000 men.

source_text: 22. When he utilises combined energy, his fighting men become as it were like unto rolling logs or stones. For it is the nature of a log or stone to remain motionless on level ground, and to move when on a slope; if four-cornered, to come to a standstill, but if round-shaped, to go rolling down.
modern_text: When you harness combined momentum, your soldiers become like boulders on a slope. A boulder sits still on flat ground but rolls when placed on an incline. Square stones stop; round stones keep rolling.
